review:
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is an absolutely beautiful, intricately detailed, amazingly realised piece of exposition. It improves upon Human Revolution in nearly every way, and I laud Edios for the amount of work and effort that went into this game, however it is clear that Square Enix cut this title into pieces to sell as DLC and future Deus Ex games and as a testing bed for the atrocious microtransactions. I had heard that Mankind Divided's main story ended quite abruptly, but when the New Game+ notification appeared and the credits began rolling I was in disbelief. I bought this game on the expectation that I was going to experience a complete story with a beginning, a middle, and an end. Mankind Divided is only the beginning. 

It is frustrating, because everything about Mankind Divided is amazing. The fusion of classical European and post modern architecture is beautiful and this world is a distinct cyberpunk that stands alone from the masses of Blade Runner inspired worlds. The combat and stealth are a massive improvement over Human Revolution, and the level design is top notch all across the board. The story (main and side quests) and its themes, despite being a bit heavy handed and not thoroughly fleshed out, have so much potential in addition to the characters that inhabit them. 

Everything about this game screams potential, it is such a shame that Square Enix had to mess it up.

You're probably wondering why I'm "Not recommending" a game that I've invested literally 5 days of my life into. For one, because Steam doesn't have a "meh" option; but mainly, because compared to its predecessor Human Revolution, this game isn't really that good.

Let's rewind to 2011, when HR was released. As a reboot of a much-loved series, it pretty much did everything right: great characters that you actually cared about, overarching plot that built to a very satisfying crescendo, and of course game mechanics that could suit anyone from the stealthiest hacker to the most gung-ho gunslinger. Yes, there were some rough edges, but they were easily forgivable given the scope and breadth of Eidos Montreal's accomplishment.

Given all that, the most burning question on my mind is: how the hell did it then take them half a decade to release what is essentially an expansion to HR? And I use the word expansion deliberately, because overall Mankind Divided feels like less of a game than its older sibling.

This is due to a lot of things. Firstly, and most importantly, instead of there being multiple cities between missions, there's one hub - Prague - that you return to repeatedly. Now, Prague definitely changes and evolves between each mission, but it doesn't really grow; you can visit almost the entirety of it right from the beginning of the game, which means that coming back to it time and time again becomes pretty boring.

That isn't helped by the fact that Prague is just plain small; there are maybe a dozen streets with about the same number of side alleys. In terms of footprint it's probably larger than HR's Detroit and Hengsha combined, but those cities were redeemed by the fact that they had more going on on roofs and multi-storey apartment blocks than they did at street level. Prague has sewers, street level, a few empty apartments higher up and... that's it.

The ridiculous load times, which were marginally acceptable in HR in 2011 but are actually offensive in MD in 2016, make this seem even worse because getting around becomes a chore. If Bethesda can ship Skyrim and Fallout 4 with multi-kilometre-square maps that have no loading times (apart from fast travel), then I fail to see why MD can't have a single seamless map for the maybe 1 square kilometre that makes up Prague. You literally have to endure a loading screen to get from one small half of Prague to the other... what? Why?

Hey, did you like the characters in HR? Too bad, because you ain't gonna see them in this game! Sarif makes three video cameos, assuming you do the side mission involving him. Pritchard? Referenced a couple of times. Malik? Referenced once, extremely indirectly. Taggart? Referenced once (yeah, he's an asshole, but still a well-portrayed one).

What we have in their place are cardboard cutouts of stereotypes that exist for no other reason than to push the plot along. You have the hacker lady who literally does nothing, the gruff leader who doesn't like it when you go off script, his second-in-command who doesn't like you, and the pilot who also doesn't like you. None of them are particularly likeable or memorable, most just get on your nerves, and talking to them really doesn't affect or alter the outcome of the game in any way. Terrible lipsyncing doesn't help to endear them either.

And then there's the villains - or should I say, villain. HR didn't do too well on this front, but at least it had more than one Big Bad and by extension, more than a single boss fight. MD has quite literally one boss fight, right at the end of the game, and you know exactly who it's going to be against BECAUSE THERE IS LITERALLY ONLY ONE CHARACTER IT CAN BE - a character you meet halfway through the game. Who is so laughably obviously the Big Bad, that all the contortions the game pulls to try to make you second-guess and think it's someone else are just cringeworthy.

"Cringeworthy" is a pretty good description of the plot, actually. This being a Deus Ex game, one would expect a meandering plot with a few dead ends, and while HR delivered, MD plays it pretty much straight. I don't have an issue with straight plots, even in a Deus Ex game - as long as they're played honest. MD doesn't do that; instead of owning its join-the-dots plot and trying to play to its strengths, it tries to obfuscate and hide that simplicity under layers and layers of unnecessary bullshit and poorly-executed misdirection, and the end result is that it just ends up feeling needlessly annoying and forced.

As for gameplay, it's HR with the rough edges mostly polished. Takedowns are easier to execute and stealthier in that Jensen actually (gasp!) attempts to hide his victims as part of the takedown animation. However, dragging unconscious enemies, or corpses, to hiding spots is just as irritating as HR, in that sometimes the dragging just stops for no apparent reason, or a limb gets stuck on something and you have to go around and pull from a different angle. And no, you still can't just PICK UP AND CARRY bodies, which would obviate this whole mess.

Combat: just like everything else in MD, the selection of weapons is similar to HR, but lesser. On the plus side you now have the option to upgrade weapons with crafting parts that can be found and bought; on the downside, some of the most powerful weapons are no longer available. Presumably this is to encourage players to rely more on the new augmentations, but Deus Ex as a series has always been about choice, and MD takes away rather than giveth. Also, no Boxguards. :'(

The new augs are pretty cool, although you can't really play with them until later in the game due to another arbitrary plot speedbump. The Remote Hacking aug in particular is probably my favourite (in fact I'd say it's almost essential), but again, it feels like something that could've and should've been in HR. There are a lot more lethal augs to complement the Typhoon, which itself is now available in a non-lethal option, and they make it possible to finish the game without using any handheld weapons, which is nice I guess.

Oh, and then there's Breach mode, which is now free sooo... doesn't really contribute to my overall sentiment towards MD. It does add some unique new mechanics and looks pretty cool in a Tron-like way, but again... free. Also microtransactions.

Finally, this game has some serious bugs - be careful with the inventory screen because often, attempting to customise a weapon from it causes the game to crash to desktop. There seems to be no rhyme or reason as to why this happens, and often attempting to customise the same weapon that caused the crash before, causes another crash - the only fix is to drop that weapon from your inventory and pick it up again. Then there's the black screen issue, whereby a single pixel goes black, then the pixels around it, then all the pixels around them... etc. until the entire screen is black and the game crashes the display driver. The "fix" is to switch your Smart Vision augment on and then off again - but good luck doing that if you're stuck in dialog or a hacking minigame. Maybe it's only a problem with NVIDIA hardware, but it's piss poor whatever way you look at it. (Yes, I have the latest patch. No, it's not overclocking or corrupted drivers.)

To conclude: on its own, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a good game, especially if you enjoy stealth. Unfortunately its predecessor Human Revolution is a great game, which makes it difficult to recommend this one unless you're a HR veteran looking for more of the same. If you're looking to start with the Deus Ex series, HR is better and cheaper; play that first before deciding whether you want to buy this.

And seriously, Square Enix? You want me to purchase mission DLC that probably should've been part of the full game? As if the microtransactions and single-use items weren't enough? Stop trying to milk this franchise and get out of Eidos' way.

It's an almost surreal experience to be writing a negative review for a Deus Ex game, after having invested countless hours in the series and enjoying them immensely (The Fall notwithstanding), but here we are. I will try to keep this short and sweet.

The game is awesome, the trademark Deus Ex feeling of having many possible pathways to solving a problem is there, the character customization is there, the great worldbuilding and lore is there (including references and callbacks to the series as whole), the excellent characters are there, and the gameplay itself is very similar to the one of Human Revolution (Which was top notch), and even improved in some areas. In short, the game is a treat and if you liked Human Revolution, you will certainly love Mankind Divided.

Now you will be thinking "But what is the problem? How come the game is reviewed negatively if it has so much going for it?"

The fatal flaw lies in the story. Not even the quality of the story itself, but that the game is clearly cut in half, in what has to be one of the worst cases of executive meddling I have ever seen, because I refuse to believe this is how it was intended from the beginning. The ending is a coitus interruptus in game form.

To put it more graphical terms (Spoilers for DX: HR coming), imagine you are playing Human Revolution, and after killing Barret, you are shown a cinematic of Adam talking to Sarif about him going to Hengsha to continue his investigation, and then the credits start to roll (30 minutes of unskippable credits, mind you, just to rub more salt in the wound).
And to add further insult to injury, two of the secondary missions in Detroit are sold as a separate DLC (Which clearly seems they were ripped from the main content), plus an extra hyper bland game mode topped off with microtransactions and lootboxes. Completely disgusting.

Deus Ex is a franchise that has a very dear place in my heart and while I certainly enjoyed the story and would like to know how it continues, I cannot abide these despicable commercial practices. Play at your own risk.

[h1]Deus Ex: Mankind Divided[/h1]
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is kind of forcing me to leave a review here, as it is one of the games that left me (incoming pun) divided about my feelings for it. I am able to absolutely recommend the game and in the same moment hating this game for what it is. This review will be (sorry in advance) divided into multiple sections, each of them covering a different motivation to play this game and why you should/shouldn't buy this game in that case.

Let's get to the sections. Ask yourself, why do you want to play this game and choose the section based on that.
Behind every reason there is a recommendation to buy or not buy, while the overall review is based on the third point.

[b]I mainly play ... 
[olist]
    [*] ... for the gameplay => buy it
    [*] ... for the story without having played Deus Ex: Human Revolution (or not caring about it) => buy it on sale
    [*] ... for the continued story of Deus Ex: Human Revolution => don't even touch this garbage
[/olist]
[/b]

[h1]I mainly play for the gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay mechanics of DX:MD are amazing. Become the ultimate nightmare of any security system with remote hacking, stealth your way with cloak augs and leg silencer, or just shoot them up with slow motion, weapon stabilisation and the titan tank aug. Every playstyle is possible, every playstyle is equaly rewarding and challenging. There are new augmentations, mostly focussed on direct attack playstyles, but I won't say no to the new guided non-lethal taser projectile, so there is enough new stuff for everyone.

Weapon handling felt way better than in DX:HR, but the amount of different types have been reduced. The typical weapon types (Pistol, Rifle, Shotgun, Sniper) are represented with multiple weapons each, and some special weapons (grenade launchers for example) are there too.

Maps are large enough to experiment with multiple playstyles, while having alot of secret ways, hidding behind obstacles or airvents. The search for them often rewards the player with valuable items, shortcuts, tactical positions or a pass around a place full of enemies.

In conclusion, while you may not get the trailer version of gameplay, but you can get damn close to it.
If you want this, you should absolutely get Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, you will have alot of good fun, amazing moments and the rewarding feeling when your plan executes perfectly.

[h1]I mainly play for the story without having played DX:HR (or not caring about it)[/h1]
The quality of the storytelling in DX:MD differs extremly between main missions and side quests, it is like two team wrote the quest, one team for the main story, one for the side quests. Sadly the good team made the side quests, which are unique, featuring the general theme of the gameworld, will let you face heavy decisions under the pressure of time and are overall done in a clever way.
The main story on the other side seems like any COD story, the bad guys, the good guys, oh no I don't know who to trust, bad guys are terrorist and so on. There are no moments of heavy decisions, no real consequences of actions and not a ending that could vary. The main story has nothing that made you think, I could have done that better or different, there is nothing you could discuss with other player, nothing that will let you regret an old decision.

So, if you are ok with a average COD style straight forward main story spiced up with really good side quest, you can go for DX:MD, but you may want to wait for a steam sale.
If you are undecided, I would recommend to read the gameplay section above.

[h1]I mainly play for the continued story of Deus Ex: Human Revolution[/h1]
You just loved, the complex story of DX:HR, how every turn, every plottwist, every new information got you totally unprepared, how this network of single story strings found together and ended in an epic final, which solved most of the questions you had, and resulted in an ultimate decision. So you are up to see what happend after the signal and what your decision have changed in the future??

I have some bad news for you ... It changed [b] NOTHING, ABSOLUTELY NOTHING! [/b]

It does not matter what you did, you end up two years after the first game and the whole world has changed. So far so good, but that means, every character you have ever met in DX:HR is gone. Well, Jensen ofcourse not and David Sarif is there for a side quest, but beside that, puff, gone, vanished, every single one.
You still remember the credit cutscene in DX:HR, you asked yourself, what the f*** was Megan doing there, I need a sequel to reveal that activity. Your sequel mentioned Megan with two damned lines of dialoque, FREAKING TWO!!!, where she is referred as "your Ex", but nothing else.

Well, I could have lived with this, but it is getting worse, ready for it?

You are still going after the group of the "Illuminati", which are involved in a terror attack, but the story and the progress you make into finding out who they are, is small, meaning non existing, but the story is getting better and you await the first boss fight, after the first really exciting level, and suddenly "Game finished". 
The [b]only boss[/b] in the game had nothing to do with all the search for the "Illuminati" and the sudden end of the game leaves you with pure frustration, the main reason why I wrote this review.

A complete meaningless story, which brings you nowhere with your question, neither from the HR nor the MD game, and it is still not the worst thing.

As all old characters vanished, new ones are replacing them. New ones, who are absolutely unremarkable. You are even forgetting the names of them, the "secret credit end scene" (you can't skip the credits, so it is only secret if you Alt+F4 out) shows one of the character and I even failed to recognize it (you can assume I suck at it, but normally I am pretty good at it).
There is so much pontential in these characters, so much stories that could be told, but no. Your new friend Alex Vega is there, but how do you met her is untold. Your new unit, your new friends, co-workers or enemies are just replacable NPCs which have close to no background. All the feeling you had for the characters in HR, are gone with the characters.
The only thing that is more generic than the characters is the story itself.
And even when some characters trying to get less generic, this is completely ruined by revenge executed in a way, you can simply miss it the whole game, by characters , who will be with you the whole time, but are only interacting with you one time to make everything worse and so on.

And now, the worst of all points.

The devs have gone full EA. The game is throwing pieces of information at you, which follow only one goal.
If I am doing a sidequest [spoiler]about my new augs and how I get them[/spoiler], I want a solution, not a questline resulting in "Some questions can't be answered yet". Are the devs kidding me, the words "but, in a new DLC" or "but, in the next game" are automatically added by the brain in that case. That has to be the dumbest and most ridiculous way of promoting a future game, which can only result in frustrated customer, which is definitly not buying the next game.
And the whole game is structured like that, not one piece of information is concluded, there are a shitload of question unanswered, everything just screams "BUY OUR NEXT GAME/DLC/EXTRA CONTENT"

So in conclusion, DX:MD is a game that has a meaningless story with blank characters in a money production maschine, that leaves the player not only way to early, with no feeling of "I could replay that better/different", but heavily frustrated, so frustatred that I will give DX:MD a negative review, something I would never thought I would do to any game, not to mention the Deus Ex Franchise.

If you are coming from DX:HR, hoping for the same/better experience, you will be deeply disappointed and frustrated. Don't say I didn't warned you.

Pros:

+ Just as beautiful as the last game, and Graphically it is far better. Hair looks good, cloth looks real... very nice.

+ Gameplay is great, better in many ways. Combat feels quicker. Mechanics like energy usage are more manageable.

+ Exploration is rewarding, with loads of little nooks and crannies to find.

+ Dialogue, animation, and cutscene quality GREATLY improved.

+ You WILL get your money's worth. 33 hours of content for myself after trying to explore every nook and cranny, and I'm convinced I missed some things as well.

+ Very well optimized for PC.


Cons:

- Story was a massive let down. Very very interesting themes were displayed, but nothing substantial was done with them. A good deal of the characters felt flat and uninteresting, and the few that ARE interesting are given no room for learning about. Even worse...

- The ending. Jesus. Let's just say the people who say it "ended abruptly" are NOT kidding. Several large questions are hinted at... and not answered. No story resolution whatsoever in a game that promised we'd "go after" the people responsible. There is also a severe lacking of choice -- only two major choices are given to you, and only one actually changes much.

Questions not answered:

* Who are the people that are taking part in this conspiracy? We get names of a few, but encounter none of them personally.
* What EXACTLY happened to Jensen? Who is responsible for his AUGs? Hinted at heavily in the cliffhanger, but despite doing thorough investigation we learn nothing.
* Who is your partner really, and what about the Juggernaut Collective/Janus?
* ???? THE CLIFFHANGER SCENE ???? WHY WAS SHE INVOLVED AND WHY DID WE NOT CONFRONT HER???


- While the new augmentations are fun to use, the unfortunate side effect is that you're either super overpowered for fights, or the enemies make you feel like fights are a drag. This is ESPECIALLY true with the "Titan Armor" aug and the "Reflective Camo" stealth aug. I ended up avoiding these augs and fights that involved them.



- ONE BOSS FIGHT. ONE. No, I don't count the side missions or the minor enemy fights. ONE BOSS FIGHT. And it was SUPER anticlimactic. 


- Prague was the only major city visited, which felt almost misleading due to how it was advertised, and downright unfaithful to how expansive the first Deus Ex was. While Prague felt enormous, the overall scale was honestly not too much larger, and I would've gladly given Prague up for new areas if given the choice.


- Controls are very clunky on PC, especially using Augmentations.


Overall:

I went between "Yes" and "No" on this one a lot. On the one hand, for both new players and Deus Ex fans, this is a very fun ride while it lasts. I believe the company should be praised for where it succeeded in improving upon the Deus Ex namesake. On the other hand, I've never felt this betrayed by a company I was SURE could do no wrong. There is no excuse for how this game's story progressed. I feel like I got a taste of the actual experience I wanted. And, at the end of the day, the "No" makes more sense, at least as a warning.

By all means, buy the game, but buy it knowing your heart is going to be torn out, especially if you liked the last game.

Most negative critics of Deus Ex: Mankind Divided concede that the Deus Ex gameplay is there - sneaking through vents, evading guards, hacking doors and computers, and swaying characters to your side using the power of conversation. That is the greatest thing DX:MD does; it take Deus Ex: Human Revolution's gameplay, and improves upon it. New augmentations, most notably the "Remote Hacking" aug, genuinely improve gameplay, and allieviate some of the problems with DX:HR. In addition, the pee-color filter is gone, which automatically makes this game look leaps and bounds better than its predecessor, even if the overall graphics are mediocre compared to other titles in 2016 (some low-poly models, occassionally fuzzy textures, nothing major really). The overall art design is excellent, and makes up for any other graphical shortcomings, however. Nonetheless, most other aspects of DX:MD are, well... lacking. The story, while complex and interesting, often feels somewhat difficult to comprehend, due to a presentation that, at points, seems jumbled and confusing. The greatest criticism most people have is its short length, especially compared to its predecessor; I didn't have a problem with this, as I spent time exploring the small, intricately crafted worlds that are the signature of Deus Ex. Through reading emails, talking to NPCs, and just paying attention to the world while exploring, stories are told. Small stories of suicides, murders, forgveness, loss are told throughout the world, if you look closely enough. Exploring the small open worlds and doing side quests makes up most of the content of the game, and if you are not interested in these things the game is not for you. Personally, I generally despise open-world games, as the side activities are generally repetitive and unimpactful. That is not the case here. Each side quest has some sort of impact. You learn about characters who feel like people instead of bland, one-note NPCs. That is the true success of Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. Offering up a variety of things to do and a world to explore using the emergent, open-ended gameplay that has made Deus Ex games so good. 

For the sake of assigning an arbitrary numerical value to my feelings on the game, I'll give it an 8/10, but take that number with a grain of salt as it really doesn't say anything about the game and whether or not you'll enjoy it and I really only assigned that number on a whim.

In summary: Buy this game if you like exploring and completeing side objectives that feel meaningful, and also if you like the emergent, stealth-based gameplay signature of Deus Ex.  Do not buy the game if you want an extremely cohesive, fully satisfying overarching narrative, or if you only want to play the main quest. You will most likely be disappointed with the main campaign.

Pros
- Good game design, fluid and easy to control and interact with the game world.
- Fun in the way choice makes a difference from how you play the game to dialogue. You can run in guns ablaze or stealth your way through everything. Kill everyone or nobody.
- Good voice acting.
- Excellent story as per the norm for Deus Ex.
- Remote hacking is stupidly fun in realtime and I kinda hope that future installments expand on this mechanic! I like it more than the main hacking minigame with the way it can be done in realtime while in combat or stealth sneaking.

Neutral
- An entire crafting system that seems sorely underutilized to the point where all I ended up crafting, ever, were biocells. It looks like they tried to create a cool user interface to craft useful items, but there's so much loot to get in general, the majority of the options are useless.
- Beat the game on the hardest difficulty setting with minimal effort. Never used a single health kit. Considering I'm hardly a decent FPS player it seems a bit too easy, but Deus Ex is known for its story dynamic, not impossibly hard shoot outs. On my next playthrough I'm just gonna sell all the health items. Storing them took up too much valuable space.
- Really stupid miniquest where you find triangles and download a cell phone app to scan and get "specials" from. I'll save you the trouble. I downloaded the app, signed onto Square Enix, and scanned two triangles, only leading to silly youtube channels, to which I felt like that was a lot of time wasted. There's another minigame for Deus Ex Go that I didn't even try, and really don't feel like I want to. This is neither a pro nor con because it doesn't hurt the game any but I really have no idea what that was supposed to add, if anything.

Cons
- Something's weird about the lip syncing. It's just... Not right. But it's not terrible and easy to ignore. It's just weird since the original Deus Ex is what pioneered lip syncing in gaming and it just comes off so weird here.
- Despite how great the story is, it ends a lot sooner than you'd expect and seems strangely narrow in scope compared to every other Deus Ex game. Even Deus Ex 2. You'll be playing through the game, expecting yourself to be barely 1/4 the way through, and suddenly the game just... Ends.
- That weird in-game store. It exists to tempt you into spending more money on the game than you already have, even though everything there can be attained legitimately through gameplay.
- On release there was a strange bug that caused tutorial text to permanently plaster onto the screen. Literally throughout the rest of the game, it stayed on your HUD. Eventually this was patched, but I still had the issue long after it was supposedly fixed. (It might be good and gone by the time of this review)

After playing through the whole game, I can 100% assure anyone buying this that the in game store doesn't offer anything you can't just get by playing the normal game. It seems to be less of a "pay to win" and more of a "pay to cheat". By the time I was at the finale to the game, I had so many Praxis kits from standard play, that I was just sticking them wherever to try out Augs I wasn't even using.

Here's where I gotta be straight, though. The game was good. But short and narrow. A lot shorter and narrower than I'd like for a triple A title at full game price. Even after doing all the side missions, and completed the main game, I felt like I only played a quarter of a real Deus Ex game and was left unsatisfied. Overall, I feel a lot more like I just played the expansion set to Deus Ex: Human Revolutions, and not a full fledged sequel.

And that's where I'm a little concerned. With the in game cash shop, I feel like that's exactly what they wanted. I can't say for sure, but are they going to gradually release DLC to "finish" the rest of the game, now, and make us pay even more? Or is this the game we got until the next one?

Now here's the thing. The game is still fun. I don't regret paying for it. But after going through it all, I feel like most people will feel very gipped and become disappointed after playing through it, and the in game store makes me extremely worried about what this will mean about the future of Deus Ex. It clearly doesn't 'harm' the game as it is right now, but it's still worrying if it grows from "pay to cheat" to "pay to win" and possibly eventually "pay to actually play the next mission" that we see on cell phones these days. Particularly since a real world cell phone app is required to partake in Triangles and bonus Praxis Kits.

Overall? It's not worth the listed price. But if you're really into Deus Ex, that probably won't matter. Still a good game, but expect it to play like a big expansion set, not a full game in of itself.

I'm of two minds about [i]Deus Ex: Mankind Divided[/i], a sequel that arguably offers up the most refined gameplay yet in the franchise, and features a metric ton of content to explore and experience.... at the cost of featuring what I feel is one of the [i]weakest[/i] plots in the franchise,

This "middle" entry of what is clearly intended to be a trilogy follows lead Adam Jensen, who (after surviving the events of the previous game in a somewhat-unexplained way) goes to Prague to work with an elite task force to investigate connections to the mysterious "powers-that-be" (the Illuminati) running a global conspiracy, and getting roped into a major plot to stop a terrorist named Viktor Marchenko from using a deadly virus to sow discord throughout the world.

If that plot sounds a little nonsensical, that's because it is to a large extent. [i]Mankind Divided[/i] makes it [b]extremely[/b] tough to get invested into many of the characters. By design or doubt, setting the game in an Eastern European city where Jensen doesn't have the same kind of contacts as he did in Detroit (most of the people in this game regard him with cool acknowledgement at best, scorn at worst) works against the narrative. You're constantly running into civilians who are rambling on about frankly inane problems or giving you scorn, and the stuff you really want to know about -- the threat of the Illuminati, the shadowy ties that bridge these organizations with certain informants and legacy characters from [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/alexngregory/recommended/238010/]the previous game[/url] -- is either relegated to a comparatively few missions, or buried in side content that you're unlikely to catch unless you're a completionist.

The game directly ties into a philosophy by series creator Warren Spector about wanting a main gameplay area that is very small (Prague is about three square blocks), but intensely packed with detail. Seriously, if you can see it in this game, you can explore, loot and check it for story info. The exploration in [i]Mankind Divided[/i] is a-one, and it's frankly absurd how much effort Eidos Montreal put into its development pipeline to crank out content for this game. Even one-off locations like Golem City and the GARM facility have breathtaking visuals and are packed full of side areas, secrets and loot to pick up. You can easily spend a good 20-30 hours just looting places in the hub world, balanced with a host of new abilities and skills revealed through the game (cutting-edge augmentations Jensen is revealed to have, which fuel part of the story).

Like [i]Human Revolution[/i], the depth of the sidequests (even if not balanced with the most interesting characters) still feel weighty and meaningful. You can miss out on some fairly-substantial side content with a wealth of lore if you're not actively exploring the world, and just like the previous games in the franchise, you can also get unique responses and solutions if you take the time do certain quests or tasks before you're asked to.

That depth of content and interactivity comes at a price, The game (much like this prequel series) is constrained by not being able to utilize certain characters effectively. Because the original Illuminati council must survive through to the events of [i]Deus Ex (2000)[/i], the plot has to center around what is effectively a sidestory involving a group of new antagonists --  and there are few characters you can really gravitate to. Outside of a handful of tertiary characters in Task Force 29 (namely, Jim Miller, Aria Argents and Smiley), the cast just doesn't come off as particularly well-explored in the conversations you have -- and the game [i]expects[/i] you to go digging around for datapads and computer entries that detail their motivations; a byproduct of a design philosophy that moved a bunch of character beats to expanded universe material.

Much has been made of the apparent "unfinished" ending, but this is the least of the game's problems (not just because the game [i]does[/i] have an ending and wraps up all the plot threads, but does so in a newscast that you might not even have realized was an ending scroll until after the fact). The biggest problem is that it wants you to get invested into a world where the stuff you want isn't explored in enough detail or only fleetingly hinted at, while the stuff you don't really want (conversations with characters who seem to be struggling to spit out words, the weird small-stakes mob fight that fuels a large chunk of the plot) and the overarching conclusion just isn't explored as effectively as it could have. You end the game with not much further understanding from where you started. You still feel like as much of an outsider with TF29 at the end as you did in the prologue, and the interactions with the Prague citizens who either have no idea what's going on or attempt to threaten/kill you aren't an effective replacement. Even the much-hyped partnership with Janus (a shadowy figure who is acting as a counterpoint to the Illuminati) isn't explored anywhere near as it well as it should have, and the game ends with a cutscene that does little to connect the dots or make this threat to the Illuminati have as much weight as it should.

That said, the game does a fantastic job with its core gameplay loops. This is a title where you will invest a lot of time looting, shooting and exploring for numerous secrets in the world, and in that respect, I can recommend the game wholeheartedly. Combat is a joy, with plenty of unique abilities to test out (including the new Rhino Armor and the non-lethal Typhoon -- finally!), sprawling bases like the Palisade Bank and GARM to explore, and plenty of challenge from enemies on the higher difficulties.

I do think [i]Mankind Divided[/i] is a worthwhile title, particularly if you're a fan of the franchise... but you must also temper your expectations, because if you're expecting a title that moves the key story beats of [i]Human Revolution[/i] forward, you're going to be disappointed.

Still, a recommended game.

[h1]Looting Simulator 2029[/h1]

[b]NOTE: At time of writing I had played 44 hours¹ of [i]Looting Simulator 2029[/i], without starting the main mission.[/b]

This game is called [i]Deus Ex: Mankind Divided[/i], which is technically correct as it is a [i]Deus Ex[/i] game where [i]Mankind[/i] is indeed [i]Divided[/i]. But the proper name for it is [i]Looting Simulator 2029[/i].

The game consists of a tutorial, then you get dumped into Prague with the initial mission "Go to work and meet your boss". I have not yet gotten around to this mission. There are lots of side-missions, and Prague is there for you to loot.

You start by waking up in your apartment. You could leave and go to work, sure. Or before you go, you could break into everybody else's apartments and loot all their stuff.

There are many ways of looting. You can break in via their side windows, or crawl through a vent to enter, or just shoot their door open. Sometimes you can make trick jumps to find hidden entrances. You can hack anything that moves, or you can collect a vast array of passwords and PINs. Once in, you can read their e-mail, steal their money, steal their guns, steal their alcohol for your massive alcohol collection, rearrange their furniture, punch holes in their walls, and create huge piles of human corpses on their bed.

Occasionally you read stuff in their e-mails that makes you feel guilty. It's a hard life in 2029 and some of it really hits you in the feels.

You sell your loot to the local arms dealer. Then you break his security, steal his personal stuff, and sell [i]that[/i] to him too.

When you're not looting, you can roam the open world and hack that, too. For example, I found a [spoiler]clandestine drug lab in the sewers[/spoiler]. It was probably connected to a mission later in the game, but who cares about that? Drugs are bad. That's all I need to know so I shot the entire thing up. You can thank me later.

There is a main storyline in [i]Looting Simulator 2029[/i] but the developers do an excellent job of making you not care. Apparently you're working for the good guys, but they're not good at all. You're told that you're loyal to characters you barely even know, which makes [i]no sense whatsoever[/i] in the [i]Deus Ex[/i] universe. Anyway you can break into (and loot) your boss' house before meeting him; it has a giant Australian flag, which means either he's bogan or the developers are ham-fisted storytellers.

For the experience of looting, stealing, and causing general chaos, [i]Looting Simulator 2029[/i] delivers.

Deus Ex: Game Divided was supposed to be a really nice sequel with interesting story and stuff like that, but it managed to fail horribly in most aspects.

Core gameplay hasn't changed - you are given freedom to achieve tasks in any way you like. This is one of the good aspects of the game. Unfortunately, quests with these tasks lead nowhere. Their outcome is supposed to influence the rest of the game, but the game ends before any quest characters can do something (aside from forgery girl, I think). Almost every NPS was made with 'I'll help you later' in mind, but they never help, because game was divided into parts.

Friendly characters have nice stories and it is almost impossible to say if they are 100% on your side. But since game is cut, there is not enough time to tell their backstories through some personal quests, which makes them dull, unlike characters from HR.

Graphics are nice, but the price you need to pay for ultra settings is too high. Levels are littered with garbage - bottles, cans, books, whatever. Every room is filled with stuff, that is supposed to show the player that real people live there. Because of that, some levels look too busy (such as Golem city); the reason is understandable, but I'd take a couple of semi-empty locations with more plot instead of detailed surroundings.

Music is good as usual, McCann hasn't lost his touch.

The game looks good in general, but abrupt ending kills all the joy. Were developers thinking that players will say 'thank you for leaving Adam in such a weird position, I will gladly wait three more years for 12 missions and 2 dlcs'? Whoever chose to split the game in parts should be fired.

Where do I start with this game? After spending around 25 to 30 hours, or perhaps even more (can't tell since I played it on offline mode), searching every corner for quests, reading all bit and pieces of informations and lore about the DX universe, and finally reached the end... I can't really articulate how I feel with the latest installment of this series. Was it Fascination? Excitement? Disappointment? Disbelief? It's all of these things.

Deus Ex: Content Divided is a fine example of such an ambitious  and truly excellent project made by talented and passionate devs has to be brought down by a load of publisher's meddling, chopping the fine game into pieces to squeeze as much money as possible. I don't blame Eidos Montreal for this, that all solely lies to Square Enix.  So, keep in mind that this review is for the game at it's current (mutilated) state, not what this game could've been.

[h1] Two Steps Forward..[/h1]

First, let's talk about the positives. Or perhaps, if you already played Human Revolution (and you definitely should), what does MD improves upon HR? And that's the gameplay and level design. It looks like Eidos Montreal really listen to user feedback and massively improves those area, especially the latter. MD is simply a bigger, bolder, and more refined game than HR, created by devs that is more confident and experienced than before. I can see they put a lot of effort to make the levels more open for possibilites to any kind of character builld. Bigger places, more vents to lurk, more "secret areas" to discover, more things to hack, and all around exploring the mission and hub area is way more fun and rewarding than HR.

Prague, is the one and only Hub in this area, yes.. One. I'll come back to it later on, since I'm going to touch the good things first. Well, Prague is way more alive than Detroit. it's bigger, and it has more content, more intricate level design, and a real treat for the eye, day and night. And that brings me to side quests, another big improvement over HR, they are more varied, interesting (both gameplay and story wise), and feels grander in scale. I found the plot and characters in some of the side quests are more interesting than the main storyline.

As for the graphic, it's simply amazing! Prague is filled with these tiny details that really improve the atmosphere and visual narrative. I'll spend two paragraphs just to describe how impressive the graphic is. So, to cut it short: It's a real neat blend of impressive graphic and amazing level design, not too empty yet never overbearing.Though the animation and lip syncing could be better.

Also, top notch sounds, soundtracks, and especially voice actings. As expected.. In exception of the weapon sounds that is.

Alright, I just finished the game, so I'll have to throw a major spoiler warning your way.
For fans of the DeusEx-franchise, that somehow didn't already play this game, I can tell you that this certainly feels like a DeusEx game. That's mainly due to the fact that this game [spoiler] has no significant bosses thrown along the way [/spoiler] and [spoiler] there is only one hub world with less side missions [/spoiler] compared to Hengsha, Detroit, etc. from DXHR. Why shouldn't you buy this game at full price? 

Because there is the possibility that you may encounter certain bugs and glitches that render the game borderline unplayable for people with only average knowledge on how to troubleshoot these issues. Save files corrupt or the game gets stuck on the loading screen/throughout cutscenes (which are used to hide loading screens). After buying this game two years after it came out, these issues are still not patched and there is no disclaimer in the troubleshooting section on the games website on how to handle them, even though at this point it's basically a FAQ. In case you wonder, you need to reduce the games graphics to a minimum and then limit it to core one in the detail section of you task manager, and after some buggy and stuttering loading/cutscenes, the game will continue, at which point you can save and reset the graphics to your prefered settings. 
Quest markers glitch out and get stuck on points you already passed, because you didn't trigger a certain event in a certain area that was avoidable if you played the game how you are intended to, exploring all the way.

Because there is a lot of unskippable content that should be skippable, and is basically just a nusiance. Starting the game takes nearly a minute because of the featured pop up screens ("powered by DAWN ENGINE" etc.). Which really gets on your nerves when you have to start the game for the 4th time in a row becaus it froze again. And lets just hope you like melodic death metal instrumentals, becaus you'll be hearing a lot of them during the credits, which are also unskippable and take about twenty -TWENTY- minutes to wrap up, all while showing the development team drunk on team events in costumes. I get that they want their game to feature them, but that was really immersion breaking for me.

The ending is a cliffhanger instead of the usual multiple ending stuff with a [spoiler] news report that shows the consequences of some of your actions, [/spoiler] and I guess they are teasing the next game with that? Problem is, it's not even a good cliffhanger. It's the most cliche cliffhanger you can come up with: [spoiler] "Random side character has been up to no good the whole time but there was no reason to believe that and it also didn't have any real impact on the story" [/spoiler].

Also, there really is no need for some elements to be in the game. Take the [spoiler] neural sub network section [/spoiler] for example. It's featured only once, and has it's own tutorial on how it works, only to never appear in the game again. It was a great idea, i liked the mechanics, but the section lasts about 10 minutes and that's it, you never use it again. 

The leveldesign is less creative than DXHR. Instead of different locations and settings, you are mostly at places you have visited before, or that look or feel the same. Think Versa Life office corridors, but all of the time, with some industrial complexes thrown in here and there. There are less partys involved in the story and some sections get stale pretty quickliy, for example [spoiler] the police shutdown of prague [/spoiler], where you'll most likely travel from hub to hub again and again, because the overarching hub world is divided by some random barricade in the middle of town, and you can only travel between the parts by subway.

So, should you play this game?
If you liked DeusEx Human Revolution, yes. The story is continued in a realistic way, and the attention to detail is a lot higher compared to DXHR. This game really rewards you for exploring, not in the way of loot, but with certain story elements and nice little touches. For example [spoiler] in the slums of Golem City youll find hints and teases at a contained story of a family, where the father killed everyone because he could not fathom to raise a child under these living conditions after his wife told him that she was pregnant [/spoiler]. If there ever is a point where you ask yourself, "I wonder if I..." - yes, you most likely can, and there will be some small easter egg along the way. As it was in DXHR, you can go the whole game without fighting, and tbh i found it easier that way. The difficulty settings only seem to affect how much damage you take and deal, so there really is no difference if you are playing the stealth or pacifist route.

But, nice little touches aside, if I had paid the full price for this game and not bought it at summer sale, I would have been severly disappointed.

Final Thoughts: The good outwheighs the bad by a small margin, and if it weren't for some severe performance problems and pacing issues, i would have definetly recommended this game. But the ones that are present are just too extreme. So it's a reluctant recommendation from me. On a scale, 35% for newbies to this great universe, 65% for hardcore fans of the series.

Mankind Divided is a great game, but unfortunately it, like BioShock Infinite, lives so deeply in the shadow of its predecessor that it becomes almost difficult to appreciate. Like Infinite, it improves on its predecessors, but only in the most superficial and unimportant ways.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution continues to be one of my favorite games of all time. The gameplay is fluid and consistent, the character abilities are well-balanced, the levels are well-designed with many paths and opportunities, the writing is strong, the pacing is consistent, the story is enticing, the art design is superb, the characters are memorable, and it all wraps up together into an enormously satisfying and replayable package.

Mankind Divided (MD) doesn’t. It doesn’t wrap up to be satisfying, but that dissatisfaction only exists in the shadow of Human Revolution (HR). Again, MD is a great game. If it’s your first experience into the Deus Ex franchise, you’ll have a good time. I recommend this game for a reason: if you buy it, you’ll enjoy it. But HR is so phenomenally better that it would take far more than the 8000 characters I’m allowed to adequately explain.

MD improves on HR in several ways, but not any way that really impacts the Deus Ex franchise. But let’s be fair, MD offers significant improvements over HR. The graphical and visual improvements are incredible. They are almost hard to overstate. Although MD released in 2016, it has environment and character textures that are better than Ace Combat 7 or Metro Exodus which released in 2019. The textures on Jensen are some of the best I’ve ever seen and the art design grows to new, even more fabulous heights. The character models are fantastic. The environments, particularly in Golem City, are incredible and display a fantastic level of affection. The graphics and design achievements are astonishing from beginning to end. The augmentations on Jensen are expanded in many ways. All of the old HR augs are here: better hacking, cloaking, social influencer, radar, armor, rebreather, and the Typhoon which has been heavily nerfed. MD adds in new “overclock” augs like remote hacking, Titan armor, Icarus dash, multi-stun wrist launchers, integrated P.E.P.S., silent wrist blade launchers, and much more.

But everything else just doesn’t hold up. The new augs are far more focused on spectacle that anything else. In a game where, at least to me, stealth and tactics are the most important, an aug that makes you impervious to rifle fire is pointless. You have no need for a multi-stun incapacitator since you have been trained (by the previous games) to use your cunning to take the guards out one by one or simply slip past them. Even if you haven’t played HR, I wouldn’t be surprised if you gravitated to the massively more useful augs like cloaking, radar, and hacking in opposition to Titan armor or other random shit. This isn’t to say that they’re useless. The remote hacking gives you new paths to use. If you really enjoy the gunplay, the Titan armor will certainly appeal. Even after fixing the overclock issues, the only new aug I used was the remote hacking because it’s the only worthwhile one that fits with a stealth playstyle.

As far as story, characters, writing, and pacing goes, there is a fair amount, just not enough to live up to HR. The story is coherent enough to move the players from one set piece to the next, the characters push the story forward as usual, the writing didn’t have many flaws, and the pacing worked until the game ended on a terrible cliffhanger. Truly, this ending was absurdly unsatisfying. In the final mission of HR, you delve into an Artic research facility, convince a megalomaniacal genius to give up on his dreams of genocide, destroy the most advanced human-AI hybrid computer ever created, stop a world-ending catastrophe that kills fifty million people, and decide the fate of human augmentation simply on your word. In MD, you go to an office building in London to stop a guy from getting poisoned, then confront a henchman of the conspiracy to stop him from blowing up an apartment building. Then it just ends. Right when the conspiracy starts to unravel and you’ve got tangible leads, roll credits. Mid-credit cutscene reveals a juicy new piece of conspiracy info. Setup for the next game which has yet to be announced or begin development. Honestly, it seems that a good 5 hours of content was cut to reserve for a game that we might not even get. 

Prague is divided up into two sections connected by a metro system, which just covers for a loading screen. It’s not uncommon to have to traverse the loading screen multiple times each time you’re doing a single side quest, and there are multiple side quests per instance of being in Prague. This becomes especially frustrating near the end of the game when martial law is called, and you have to sneak everywhere in Prague. You end up spending more time in the metro than you do in Metro Exodus.

I recommend this game because, by all objective measures, it is a decent game. If you’re a Deus Ex fan, you should play this because you’re a fan and it’s required. If you’re new to Deus Ex, I would recommend HR first, but this isn’t the worst place to start if you’re set on it.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is an unnecessary game. Eidos-Montreal wrote a self contained banger of a story with the first game, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, a worthy successor to the original, there was no need to make yet *another* game, especially with Jensen, but they came back to the drawing board anyway, only to have Square Enix pull the rug out from under them. They were told to split the game they were making into two halves, so Square could ship it as a trilogy.

So they released DE:MD, got to work on the second half, were moved from that to multiple other projects, some failures, some not, then sold off to Embracer, where they were supposedly making the third game again, but were then wracked with layoffs when Embracers billion dollar deal fell through. Eidos-Montreal now plays second fiddle to her sister company Crystal Dynamics.

So this game should be bad right? It was quite literally hamstrung during development.

You finish what feels like the end of the mid game arc, and then abruptly, credits roll. Out of everything, this alone is the only jarring part. AND, the only negative thing I have to say about the game.

Everything else is Eidos-Montreal at arguably its strongest. Everything from the first game was improved upon to the nth degree. The movement and controls got a full face lift, the environments are more focused and feel more lived in. The powers actually give you a wide variety of focused gameplay styles now. You can slip through areas completely unknown, or you can blaze through them with modified SMG’s and take shotgun blasts like a wall.

Guns can still be modified with scopes and silencers, but now they can also be upgraded through crafting materials. Damage can be upped, capacity can be upped, etc. Crafting actually isn’t obnoxious in this game, you have one resource aptly named “Crafting materials” that you will find in abundance as you scour through every drawer and locker, and you can use it to craft (my beloved) multi-tools, nano blades, etc. It’s not overwhelming, it’s well implemented and compliments the game well by not getting in your way.

Every limited open world game should take a page out of this game for how the team designed Prague. The city is a character all in itself. There are nooks and crannies and secrets to be discovered everywhere. It’s not a “living and breathing” city like you might find in open world sandbox games, npc’s aren’t really milling about, but it’s a city that engages you like a puzzle. You will find vents that connect you from relevant act 1 areas to relevant act 3 areas. It is the best kind of maze, and pro tip, getting the boosted jump upgrade early lets you bypass SO MUCH.

Prague is truly stunning. The muted colors compliment each other well. It helps that throughout the 3 acts, the city changes in completely different ways and the colors that use wash out the city in a noir kind of way. The game fits a highly specific vibe, it hits the same notes as walking the rainy streets of New Mombasa in Halo ODST. What compliments it the most is the soundtrack. It’s no surprise that you can find countless “work/study/write to Deus Ex MD” playlists and compilations on YouTube. Stand out tracks include “TF29”, “Church of the Machine God”, “Golem City: RVAC Row”.

The side quests are better. Half of them don’t even get a resolution, but they queue up what would’ve been the next portion so well, you can almost anticipate where they were going to go.They feed into the main storyline perfectly, a lot of them end up reflecting either Jensen or add to the core principles of the game.

The main story is exceptional, top notch really. Had Eidos been left alone to make the remaining section of the game, it would’ve been grand. Even better than the first (they have a bunch of teasers in the game about where they would’ve gone with it, and some crazy reveals. Read the theories online after you beat the game to see what could’ve been.)

Ultimately, this is a series about a man on a crusade of one. He’s up against the most powerful individuals in the world, and from the context of the original Deus Ex game, we know he inevitably fails. Adam Jensen is a cog that eventually gets crushed by the machine. And yet, for someone who always has his eyes on the bigger picture, he never misses the forest for the trees. You help so many different individuals in both of these games, especially in the second one. You can definitively say that Adam Jensen is a force for good, and even though his crusade fails, that doesn't change just how many lives he improved along the way. An admirable way of moving forward in life.

I feel like rating this game would almost do it a disservice, but 5/5, easy. A “5” with me telling you that this game, and its predecessor had irrevocably changed me for the better, and will stick with me until it’s my time for the journey into the unknown.

Depending on what you look for in video games (and especially one carrying the weight of the Deus Ex franchise), Deus Ex: Mankind Divided will either be thoroughly enjoyable experience or a complete let-down. If you come to the game expecting a fun, RPG/ immersive sim, you will find a lot to enjoy. On the other hand, if you want a meaty story to bite into, you will leave starved.

To quickly get the negatives out of the way, the story leaves next-to-no impact. While a story full of international conspiracy, cover-ups, and terrorist attacks, should be gripping, the plot is simply bland and forgettable. Nothing in the story detracts from the game, mind you, but it certainly doesn’t add. The events of the plot never seemed to carry much weight and just served to advance to the next mission. Just a few weeks after playing, I cannot name a single character besides the protagonist, Adam Jensen. 
	
Fortunately, this problem mostly sticks to the main plot. Some of the side stories are quite interesting. For example, in one early on, you discover an illegal drug distribution ring operating in Prague, the game’s main location. When divorced from the main plot, the writing quality greatly improves. The writing, in general, creates a world which seems to be inhabited by actual people. Many times, I would find a ‘pocket secretary’ (a sort of phone) with messages from coworkers complaining about how “for the last time, the code to the door is 1645! You cannot be this dumb!” Or you find yourself sorting through emails and you discover the petty feuds between coworkers. In these moments, the writers were allowed to have fun making a world which felt interconnected. Often emails would be referenced in later emails on different terminals and you could piece together a story about what happened to the poor guy in apartment number whatever. 
	
On the gameplay front, Mankind Divided offers great improvements over Human Revolution. For starters, the city of Prague is an immensely detailed hub-world where most buildings can be entered and offers many routes to discover off the beaten path. The levels in general always offer more than one way to achieve any objective and the exploration constantly feels like a treat. The level design takes a lot of inspiration from metroidvanias where pathways constantly loop back on themselves in interesting, surprising ways. The augments have also been tweaked to be more useful overall. Some abilities which were nearly useless in Human Revolution see regular importance in Mankind Divided. Pro tip: the high-jump ability is hands-down one of the most useful skills in the game.
	
If you’re a fan of the series (especially Human Revolution) you will find a lot to enjoy here. If you’re new to the franchise and want a story-rich game, you would be better served elsewhere. However, if you want a fun stealth/ action game to explore in, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided will more than scratch that itch.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
If you are a die-hard Deus Ex fan who has completed every other game and is jonesing, [b][i]and[/i][/b] you’ve got a beast rig that can handle a modern [i]Crysis[/i] then, sure, why not. Otherwise, wait on this one.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
The game is gorgeous, and as of the opening missions, the world building seems solid, [i]i.e.[/i] it felt like a worthy successor to what they’d built up in [i]Human Revolution[/i]. Taking place only 2 years after HR, the fallout of that game’s conclusion (with the exception of one of the ending choices, naturally) is the focus, and it is nice for a game to take a step back to let the world really speak for itself.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
Upon starting up the game – besides seeing that the default settings for my hardware got 45fps – I looked around and found a hidden item, which gave me a proprietary QR code. This requires a smartphone app to read. Said app is also necessary for monitoring in-game stats like how many alarms you’ve triggered, etc. (This is necessary info for various achievements, etc.) This is not only a bit of a pain, but also reduces how future-proof the game is, as it is unlikely that SquEnix is going to maintain an App and the game, especially considering how poor the support is so far (see below).

This game also can’t be discussed without bring up microtransactions. Not only did it have an overbearing pre-order system, which essentially held content to ransom, but the current DLC options – for a game that has been out for well over a year now – include single-use items. I repeat: In a single-player game, they are selling single-use items like ammunition for real money. This issue really came to a head this year (2017), and while it’s not as egregious as [i]Battlefront II[/i] or [i]Shadow of War[/i], the ability to pay real money for Praxis points to make the game easier is disgusting. Either you’ve balanced your game properly, or you haven’t. Arguments about “letting people control their gameplay” with money is, and always will be bullshit.

SquEnix’s greed has made the death of a franchise an annual event now. They killed [i]Deus Ex[/i] in 2016, and [i]Hitman[/i] in 2017, but unlike the latter, they didn’t cut the actual developer loose to work on their IP as they saw fit. (It would be nice for a [i]Hitman[/i], or even [i]Human Revolution[/i] style, “Director’s Cut,” but as long as [i]DX[/i] is under SquEnix’s grubby little thumb, this is unlikely.) The worst victim in this case seems to be the ending of [i]MD[/i]. In order to squeeze more money out of the fans, that was held back, to be released as DLC or a sequel, or something. But because this game did not meet sales expectations – which were kneecapped by the publisher’s own release plan – that may never happen.

[h1]The Unforgivable[/h1]
For a so-called “AAA” studio release to be this poorly optimized – again, 15 months after release at the time of writing – is unforgivable. On an overclocked GTX 1070 & an overclocked i5 6600K, I had to turn down default settings to hit 60fps at 1080p. That could be forgiven as the game being “before its time,” and too beautiful for computing hardware of today. What can’t be forgiven is the fact that the game crashed twice during the opening mission alone. I was willing to overlook the shitty DLC & microtransaction system, and even the lacklustre ending, but if the act of [i]playing the game[/i] doesn’t feel good, then there is [b]no point[/b]. I would rather wait years to either get a version of this game that corrects issues, and removes the garbage, or to have some future hardware iteration that can just brute-force this to work properly. By that time, the game should cost considerably less, to boot.

The game, [u]in its current state[/u], is such a disappointment it leaves a bitter taste in my mouth. Luckily the cinematic opening and having to restart the opening mission twice did not take longer than Steam’s refund window, because, even at 85% off, I was glad to have my money back on this.

Poorly written and uninteresting, this is a disappointment after Human Revolution.
Jensen's character and personality is highly railroaded, in conversations he's constantly going off on tangents and rants of his own with no dialogue options or input from the player. There are very few opportunities to take a side or make a choice that would develop Jensen's character into something different. Jensen has already chosen a side and has made up his mind on all the issues in the game, the player's just there to listen to him talk.
The secondary characters from the previous game are almost completely gone, with the exception of a couple calls from Sarif. They are replaced by, what are from the player's perspective, complete strangers despite the game insisting that Jensen has some sort of history/relationship with them. Would have been nice to get some insight into it like the intro with Megan, or build it up a bit like it was with Pritchard and Malik... unfortunately, you don't get that.
The story has little nuance as is amusingly black-and-white, with no shades of grey. Who the good guy is and who the bad guys are is obvious from the second they appear on the screen, and their motivations are just as bland and obtuse. Bad cyborg with gun-arm man wants to blow stuff up and kill people because he is evil. Illuminati want to take over the world and control everyone because they want power. Good guy hacker man is good because he wants to help everyone and doesn't like bad things. 
The ideas that augments are dangerous and the perspective of people that suffered from them and are motivated to oppose them, like Sanders in HR, are swept aside almost completely, and are only spouted by obviously evil and corrupt characters as an excuse to oppress the augmented. The fact that every single aug went berserk and tried to slaughter innocent people only a couple years ago is more often served as propaganda made to make people irrationally hate the augmented than a genuine fear and concern that augments pose a danger and something like that could happen again (in fact, I don't remember a single character mentioning the possibility of "the incident" repeating, making every existing aug a potential threat in the future. And the augs themselves rarely seem concerned that they could be controlled and sent into a frenzy against their will, one would this it's a terrifying concept that hangs over them like Damocle's Sword as long as they have the augments.")
Gameplay-wise the game is less intuitive. The recharging battery is still only enough for one takedown at a time. The new augmentations require a lot of resource consumption or micro-managing, with only a couple being useful in a consistent way throughout the game. The weapon customisation has practically not built on what was in HR, in fact the variety of weapons is smaller (The RPG, Plasma Rifle, Crossbow, Laser, Heavy rifle are not even in the game), as are the attachments to them. There is, as far as I've found... One new weapon. That's it. HR managed to do just fine without this sort of unnecessary micro-managing somehow.
The "customisation" that is present is just a basic "do more damage", "hold more ammo" etc improvement to stats. Something that the first game didn't really need and this one doesn't benefit from either.
Even more micro-managing is introduced with new ammunition types, stuff like AP, EMP and regular ammo for most weapons clogs up the already limited inventory space. Even worse is that there are several "unique" or special varieties of weapons that take up their own inventory slots and will only use a specific type of ammo. eg. An EMP-only combat rifle, an AP-only Revolver, battle rifle, shotgun etc. Which likely won't see much use because they can't use the majority of the ammunition you find and will become obsolete as soon as you run out. This just brings more micro-managing ammunition types, more clutter of inventory space, less usage of the actual weapons as you're forced to throw them away or sell them because you don't have the space to carry and try them all out.
Level design is uninteresting, with almost all the game spent in wandering the streets of Prague, sometimes breaking into a garage or a single-room apartment or something. There are very few large buildings or facilities to infiltrate or explore like the bank, G.A.R.M. and the final mission. Sneaking around is by far the most effective way to complete any objective, making the aforementioned weapons even less appealing, But if you do decide to partake in some combat you'll likely just sit in one spot and pick off the enemies one by one until it's over, even more so than in HR, because the AI will be aware of your presence and exact location almost straightaway and will try to swarm you, so those that prefer silenced weapons and picking off enemies from afar while they search for them will be disappointed. Once again, HR delivered on level variety and exploration much more competently, strange that the sequel didn't measure up.

This one hurts, but I can't lie to myself. The previous game, Human Revolution is by far my favorite in the series. Despite some occasional visual oversights and gameplay irritations, I loved it. It was a GOTY candidate for me, for sure.

So obviously I was hyped for this sequel. I wanted to know where Adam Jensen would end up after every augmented human went temporarily berserk before his very eyes. Well apparently he just ended up switching employers, and never had another exciting day in his life ever again. 

I don’t know what it is about this new game but I can’t find anyone interesting, any quest compelling, or any reason to bother playing ball. I did, though. I beat it. I did every side quest I could reasonably find. But there’s just no….CHARM in this sequel. This entire experience felt like a typical Tuesday for this guy compared to the last game.

At least in the last game we had an endearing, if not a bit weasley bossman. We had a girlfriend to rescue. A hackerman stereotype who’s snark honestly made me laugh a few times. We had a spunky and cute “Flygirl” to our “Spyboy” who saving the life of actually was the greatest challenge in the game, but there was no fucking way we were letting her die. And of course we had a cataclysmic ending, multiple endings in fact, that left the player deeply considering their choices.

And here we have a new game….that essentially just feels like we’re just playing a cop of sorts. Many mundane, uninspired tasks to play through. UNINSPIRED is really the key word about this game. I really only cared about two moments in the entire playthrough, and both were sidequests. One with a crazy cat lady resident, and another with an underground rebel news network. Everything is quite snappy. Unfortunately it pushed a mobile app on you if you care to find out what these weird triangle items are you keep finding. The app is garbage and can’t even properly play the developer interview videos you are unlocking with your efforts.

It comes with a 30 minute mini campaign that is insanely boring and basically one level to explore, that fills a story gap around the 1 hour mark of the core campaign. I won’t bother purchasing the two short DLC campaigns, even if one of them brings back Pritchard. Besides that you have this super odd mode called Breach.
