[i]Deus Ex: Mankind Divided[/i] (hereafter [i]Deus Ex: MD[/i] for short) is a first-person stealth-action role-playing game. It offers a lot of content to the player who enjoys such a mix of genres and it certainly gets a lot of things right, but unfortunately, it also gets some things wrong. In the end, I feel the good things far outweigh the bad and I'd rate this game very highly as it offered me dozens of hours of immersive fun. 

[h1]Story[/h1]

[quote]Note: [i]Deus Ex: MD[/i] continues the story of [i]Deus Ex: Human Revolution[/i] and the story from the books by James Swallow (mainly [i]Deus Ex: Blacklight[/i]). Don't worry if you're not familiar with the people and the events from these stories. You'll find a 'Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Recap Video' in the game menu. Furthermore, past events are explained briefly during the game's story, you can read about it in eBooks you find in the game and you get some summaries in the game's loading screens.[/quote]

After the protests and riots as a result of the polarization between the augmented and the non-augmented humans that was the focus of the story of [i]Deus Ex: Human Revolution[/i], which climaxed when a terrorist organization triggered all augmented people to go into a murderous frenzy (now referred to as 'the aug incident'), the world is even more divided. Both groups of people are extremely suspicious of each other and basically, the whole situation is a powder keg. 

A couple of organizations claim to represent the interests of their respective group of people and they either demand equal rights for the augmented or a limitation of those rights in the wake of 'the incident'. Some of these organizations are extremist groups or even terrorist groups. 

When a train station in Prague gets blown up by one of these extremist groups, an augmented Interpol agent called Adam Jensen is sent to investigate. He finds himself in a city that's increasingly weary of augmented people. The local authorities even have augmented people shipped off willy-nilly to a seedy housing complex called 'Golem City' by its inhabitants, adding to an already explosive situation.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

[i]Deus Ex: MD[/i] is mainly meant to be played as a stealth action game. But you can play it as a first-person shooter, too, if you prefer a more aggressive and harder route.

Don't get me wrong. Gun combat in this game is certainly enjoyable. There are different types of guns, skills to enhance your shooting skills and defense, different types of ammo and upgrades for your weapons. However, in the first part of the game you won't be equipped to survive more than five seconds of actual combat, so you'll automatically turn to sneaking, at least partially. 

The whole sneaking system, which is pretty much the essence of [i]Deus Ex: MD[/i]'s gameplay, is exciting and fun. You analyze the opponents' positions and patrol routes and try to single out one of them to sneak up to without being seen by his comrades or by security cameras. You then press a button on your keyboard/controller to silently eliminate him. Finally, you drag the body out of sight of any remaining patrols or security cameras.

The main thing that makes [i]Deus Ex: MD[/i] enjoyable is its impressive level design. The main hub, the city of Prague, is huge by comparison to the two smaller hubs in [i]Deus Ex: Human Revolution[/i]. There's also much more exploring to do as the Prague hub has a lot more optional (i.e. not quest-related) areas. 

The areas you're supposed to sneak (or fight) your way through have been designed with the utmost care. There always seem to be at least three ways leading to your target. Which ways are available to you depend on your creativity and the augmentations (skills) you decide to invest in. You can crawl through vents, move aside heavy objects that are blocking the way, jump down from great heights, punch through weak spots in walls, remote-hack cameras or turrets to give you time to pass them undetected, hack locked doors, hack computers to disable security systems, use your resistance to gas or electricity to pass through corridors that would otherwise be unpassable, and more.

It's too bad the hacking minigame is based on luck. You can increase your chances by investing in skills and by using consumable items, but it remains a minigame based on luck. So you will be reloading a lot. I would have preferred a minigame that relies on logical thinking or on dexterity, especially since you play the hacking minigame a couple of hundred times.

Another piece of bad news is [i]Deus Ex: MD[/i] has a lot of bugs. They're all minor bugs so no game-breaking issues, but they're annoying by themselves and even more so because they are plentiful. We're talking about clipping issues, rendering issues, problems with scrolling the map, no mouse scrolling during the hacking minigame, controls sometimes not responding, drawers that are shown as lootable but you can't interact with unless you reload, quest markers that point to the wrong place, merchants who keep saying you're wasting their time when you only sell items (and later on even when you do buy stuff from them), and so on. Together, all these small issues make the game feel unpolished, especially after a couple of patches that already fixed a bunch of bugs. 
 
[h1]Graphics and sound[/h1]

The game's graphics look good enough for a current-gen game. Still, I wasn't overly impressed with the graphics but that's probably because I ran the game on 'high' settings, so maybe that's a far cry from the 'very high' and the 'ultra high' settings.

Speaking of Far Cry, the voice acting is top-notch. Especially Elias Toufexis, who voices protagonist Adam Jensen (and who has voiced main characters in Far Cry, Splinter Cell and Assassin's Creed). He delivers a voice that's a cross between Doug Cockle's Geralt of Rivia and Christian Bale's Batman, and he manages to put some humanity in an otherwise cool-as-ice Jensen, who is more machine than man, after all.

The music sounds wonderful. It's subtle and atmospheric, exactly as it should be.

[h1]DLC and Breach Mode[/h1]

The story DLC isn't integrated in the main story, even though that would have been easy to accomplish, and they are overpriced for most people's taste. 

The equipment DLC add a few weapons that you can easily do without, and some consumables that are one use only, so you can only use them in one playthrough.

Breach Mode is [i]Deus Ex: MD[/i]'s version of the [i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] games' Raid Mode. It's really a separate game in which you're put in an environment where the mechanics and skills are the same as in the story mode, but the only goal is to go through some sort of endless 'gauntlet levels' in order to get increasingly better skills, weapons and weapon upgrades.

[h1]On Steam's extra features[/h1]

[i]Deus Ex: MD[/i] has 9 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 5 while running the game.

The Steam Achievements are varied and challenging. Getting 100% achievement completion for [i]Deus Ex: MD[/i] is difficult because:
[list]
[*] all but one achievements of the main game are missable;
[*] the achievements for the DLC are listed even if you don't own them;
[*] there are a bunch of achievements for the Breach Mode of the game, which won't be everybody's cup of tea;
[*] at least one achievement requires a second playthrough as the perma-death difficulty only unlocks after finishing the game in one of the three basic difficulty modes;
[*] some achievements require constant attention and some planning ahead, like 'find all 75 eBooks', 'finish the game without killing anyone' and 'finish the game without triggering any alarms'. For the last two achievements, it's too bad they still didn't implement some form of status screen that shows whether you killed someone or tripped an alarm in your current game, as both of those things may happen without you noticing it until the credits roll and the achievement doesn't pop up.
[/list]

As someone whose favorite game is the original Deus Ex and a massive critic of Human Revolution's more streamlined level design and mechanics, I went into Mankind Divided with the lowest expectations possible. I had heard terrible things about this game's pre-order and marketing, as well as the general consensus leaning more towards the idea that this is an inferior game compared to Human Revolution.

Truth is, after beating the game, my expectations were greatly surpassed. Not only is this a rare case of a good modern Immersive Sim (something I'm also not a huge fan of) but also a great entry in the Deus Ex franchise with enough connections to the original game and fun mechanics that will encourage repeated playthroughs to experience all its different playstyles.

Mankind Divided's level design, side missions, gameplay, and art style are all top-notch and should serve as an example for what a modern triple-A game should be like. The different augmentations you can obtain while playing the game really enhance the experience and combat to a whole other level. Nothing is more satisfying than using all your different augmentations in tandem to bypass or eliminate large amounts of enemies. The game really showcases true expression in which upgrades you choose to invest your Praxis Kits in and which ones you do not, especially with Adam Jensen's new experimental augs which quickly became one of my favorite aspects of the game.

Where the game falls flat, in my opinion, is probably its story. It feels like a middle entry in a much larger plot, and it sort of ends when things are getting interesting or leading up to the events of the original Deus Ex.

As a final note, many people say this is best enjoyed as a stealth game. Honestly, screw that. Embrace the true power of Adam's new augmentations, get the strongest weapons, go guns blazing, and have fun just being a god among men. This is not only a great Immersive Sim but also a great game overall, and that's coming from someone who went into this expecting to hate it.

After playing Deus Ex Human Revolution (Predecessor of Mankind Divided) multiple times, being one of my favorite games, I looked forward to Mankind Divided. In short, Human Revolution a game with multiple paths and options, with a great storyline of conspiracy which you have to discover and uncover yourself. You can really invest yourself into the story.
The start of the game was, in my opinion, one of the weak parts: you're dropped right into contact with multiple characters and situations of whom you've never heard of before (except in the trailers), but whom are apparently well known to the main protagonist. While these connections were introduced rather sloppy, you do get to know them about two hours in. 
The storyline overall is very good. The feeling of being kept in the dark was fun, as it led to many surprises to which you can react. The main story changed the rest of the universe as well, which makes you feel like you are really making an impact on it. The story connected to the previous games as well (With Human Revolution being the past and the original Deus Ex as the future) in a way that made sense. Multiple sidequests with connection to Adam Jensen, being old aquaintances or connected to the atmosphere and his opinion about them. Some sidequests are randomly found, which made solving those mysteries much more enjoyable.
The atmosphere of the game is great, you see the division of "Naturals" and "Augs" and the results because of it everywhere around you. The main protagonist can also strike up multiple conversations on the workfloor with colleagues, which made them feel like more than just random NPC's by having discussions or building up friendship even if it doesn't alter the storyline at all.
The combat has been vastly improved; in Human Revolution the normal pistol was an unchallenged king out of the other weapons, but in Mankind Divided each weapon has their own merit (Some large open fields for the sniper rifle, different types of special ammunition, effective range and piercing, etc). Gunfights have more glasscannon than bullet sponge enemies, which is something I enjoy as well. Adam's health felt quite low, but I haven't tried out the Titan shields yet, which should give Adam Jensen a much higher survivability. Some situations felt poorly planned, some ambushed start you in a 3v1 situation without cover, making it hard to find cover or take them out fast enough on the highest difficulties.
The stealth system was improved as well with multiple phases like panic, hostile and searching. Although this was already present in the predecessor, it's more fleshed out in Mankind Divided by making the stages of NPC's known from the start. The ability to pull enemies with you behind cover in hand to hand combat also was a quality of life improvement, making the game react more to your intentions (Because you almost always want to hide bodies).
The amount of possible paths to locations was even bigger than in Human Revolution, making every playstyle viable instead of a choice between vents and following the main path; almost every floor was a new maze of possibilities.
The cityhub felt a little less diverse than Human Revolution which had a wider variety of scenery with Hengsha and Detroit, as Mankind Divided only has Prague and a small moment in Golem City. It was, however, much more impressive than it's predecessor as the area's changed much more because of new events. Shops are all over the city, which made selling items and buying new ones quite easy. Shop interaction was kind of flawed; you have to sit through 4 one-liners of the NPC which narrow down to "I sell items. Please buy items?" before you get access to their computer (which contains their wares), and exiting wants you to confirm your exiting multiple times.
There is only one bossfight in Mankind Divided compared to Human Revolution's multiple, but it doesn't feel like this game is lacking them. 

TL;DR:
[list]
    [*]Atmosphere feels rich and is vastly visible.
    [*]Combat and stealth is improved and feels great with multiple options.
    [*]Storyline is good, albeit the earlygame connection is weak.
    [*]Possible paths have increased tremendously, making even more playstyles viable.
[/list]
It's a great game, a worthy successor of the earlier Deus Ex franchise.

Mankind Divided might well have been (hopefully not permanently) the last nail in the coffin of the Deus Ex franchise, but I’ve always had a special appreciation for the game.

The IP has been dead for several years, and although the industry tends to zombify such things, i don’t hold out much hope for a new title with the budget and care it deserves.

Anyway, for better or worse, whether clumsy, incomplete, unintentionally comical, and slightly broken, Mankind Divided is an excellent game.

Undoubtedly, a considerable improvement compared to Human Revolution, even if the intelligence factor, when it comes to narrative, is almost equally matched by stupidity.

Relatively more self-contained than the others, Mankind Divided has a more modest structure, placing most of its missions in a sandbox located in Prague instead of an intricate journey around the world.

Prague is a masterclass in design. A relatively large, complex, interconnected area, perfectly readable and easy to visually memorize, full of secrets and rewards for the curious and attentive. Exploring it is a complete delight.

As one of the best examples of level design in immersive sims, Prague perfectly accommodates all traversal options available in the player’s skill tree, expands as new abilities are unlocked, and presents all its spaces functionally and purposefully, serving both gameplay and the narrative aesthetic the game communicates.

It’s a dense playground of options and well-set, accommodating all the game systems and its narrative content in a way that never feels repetitive or restrictive. The dynamism of the gameplay drowns out any sense of boredom.

I’ve finished the game three times, and this last one, I spent hours freely exploring every bit of the scenery, looking for additional rewards, side stories, and secrets, besides trying to do all the main and secondary material. And I still believe there are things left to discover, new strategies to experiment with, and different solutions to old puzzles.

This is the type of game where you always feel you have multiple options available at every minute. And you never get lost or stuck for too long when encountering a problem. You’re always rewarded for your creativity.

The systemic nature of the game, with easily identifiable enemies and obstacles and clear rules for manipulation, generates fantastic emergent situations that can easily be worked to your advantage. If you know what you’re doing (or not), it’s fantastic to be surprised by things you didn’t even know could be done.

Objective markers are the most redundant thing you’ll find here. And I strongly recommend turning them off. Reaching objectives guided by the design of the environment is always viable and generally more rewarding. Your attention is golden.

Let the game guide you, absorb the atmosphere and details. Enjoy the experience without rushing.

The levels outside Prague are well-made too, but they don’t linger much, so it’s hard to instill a deeper appreciation for their experiences since most of the game’s content is located in the city.

The mix of combat and stealth remains at the expected level of competence. You have to tolerate a bit of jank in some things, but overall it’s excellent.

Combat is sharp and consistent, with lethal, relatively intelligent enemies, little ammunition available, and no random respawns or artificially designed areas to accommodate shootouts (making any fight in the game feel more organic and dynamic). Each fight can be costly, and you’re discouraged from head-on confrontations whenever enemies appear.

Play the game on hard (Give me Deus Ex or I Never Asked for This), and you’ll have to respect the enemies and be as lethal and precise as possible whenever things go wrong. 

Stealth works especially well, with a cover system optimized for more stealthy operations and a myriad of new tools, both lethal and non-lethal, to assist in these endeavors.

Jumping from one to the other is smooth, and combined with the movement mechanics, you have versatile and always fresh gameplay. Among the versions of the game I’ve had, I must have played almost 100 hours and still haven’t gotten tired of how fun it is to navigate this game.

The other aspect of the game, and perhaps the most precarious part of the experience, has to do with the conversations and ultimately with the narrative itself.

The writing isn’t necessarily bad, but it’s very inconsistent, featuring characters with artificial voices and personalities without much nuance or credibility to take their speeches seriously. It’s not uncommon to find characters whose intentions are hard to decipher or understand why they behave in certain ways or occupy certain positions within organizations. If the performances were more competent and the tone more identifiable, some of these figures might not sound so strange and out of place.

The plot is relatively competent, presenting a simple but multifaceted conspiracy connected to the sociopolitical tensions of the universe’s background. 

This background is a bit forced to evoke allegories about racial segregation, apartheid, and the like.

It’s somewhat poorly thought out and incomplete, with high-class citizens or those associated with large corporations being racialized, systematically oppressed, and isolated in ghettos and concentration camps, only to be ultimately eradicated from society. 

All this within two years… It’s a stretch, to say the least. Hardly convincing.

It’s as if everyone suddenly became extremely stupid and adhered to the clumsy puritans of Human Revolution, hating prostheses and implants simply because they went through a collective trauma, whose main victims are exactly those they want to isolate.

A bit of collective hysteria or angry discussions about regulation? Yes, that I accept. Racializing people with prosthetics, no matter which kind? Is just too ridiculous.

“Cyberracism”/apartheid seems like interesting and provocative ideas to explore in this universe, but the execution wasn’t very good, and the result doesn’t say much about the subject itself, even though once you dive into the details of the newspapers, books, and articles, it proves to be much less stupid than it initially appears.

They were more successful in addressing loaded issues through aesthetics and at least tried to extract real discussions from the allegory. About how the political game would work around such a case and what the sociopolitical and economic implications of such a gigantic schism would be. How billionaires, mega-corporations, and other power figures would take advantage of the crisis to thrive, and so on.

It’s bad, but not as bad as Detroit Become Human.

They probably failed due to a lack of time to tie up the details or a more incisive commitment to the argument. But hey, at least the subject is not as abstract as in Human Revolution.

In my book, any story that invites its consumers to think about sociopolitical issues at any level, even if somewhat clumsy, is already better than the vast majority of power fantasies we see out there.

And Mankind Divided is a power fantasy about being a super cyborg spy who shoots blades from his arms and steals beer from his neighbors… So it’s the best of both worlds, i guess.

The gameplay more than sustains the experience, which otherwise would be somewhat mediocre. The graphics are passable, the music is wonderful, and in the end, it doesn't leave much to be desired.

I definitely recommend it.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided

I have no doubt that Mankind Divided is a true masterpiece of the tenth art. At first, I thought it was just another poorly made generic FPS. I tried playing it four times, and only on the fourth attempt did I finally understand that it was, in fact, an RPG. That changed everything. This is how the game should be approached: not as a shooter, but as a deep role-playing experience.

What fascinated me the most was the developers’ decision to create a small and dense world instead of a vast, generic, and empty open world, which is unfortunately typical in modern games. The environment in Mankind Divided is incredibly detailed, full of notes and rich lore.

I love literature, and being able to read all those in-game notes made me genuinely happy. It brought the world to life. You start to feel like that universe truly exists, with its own history and depth.

I just finished the main campaign and I’m honestly disappointed because the game ends abruptly, and to this day there is no continuation. That’s a shame, because this is a work of art. A game with this level of immersion should never be thrown away or forgotten.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution, this game's predecessor, was, and still remains, THE game that brought Deus Ex back to life as a franchise. As thought-provoking as it was entertaining, Human Revolution still boasts some of the best gameplay, world-building, character development, and overall writing I've personally experienced in gaming thus far. So, how does Mankind Divided stack up? In my opinion, it's a simultaneous step up AND down.

Gameplay-wise, there are [i]serious[/i] sweeping quality of life improvements made across the board from Human Revolution, and ones that still hold up almost a decade later. Everything from hacking to movement, weapon handling, customization, dialogue, and player abilities has been honed and refined to a T. However, I [i]wish[/i] I could say the same for the game's quality assurance and control. For whatever reason, I encountered various bugs that would either freeze the game, or just outright prevent it from loading and force me to alt-tab, bring up the task manager, and kill the game. There was also a couple instances where characters would get stuck on chairs or other parts of the environment they're meant to interact with. Bit of a nitpick, but even installed on an M.2 SSD, the initial load times could be quite lengthy, too.

Visually, the game is quite detailed and realistic, even if those details come at an unnecessary performance cost. However, overall character design, whilst incredibly detailed, is quite muted for new characters compared to Human Revolution. They're rather [i]bland,[/i] and suffer from not having anywhere near as much screen presence or memorable visual traits as their Human Revolution predecessors. Also, with the exception of a proud few, much of them also either don't do much in their introductions, or really endear themselves to the player, leaving them to have to learn more about them as they go along. Thankfully, what little characters return from the previous game get some appropriate, if at times [i]jarring[/i] visual upgrades. (Yes, Pritchard, I'm looking at you.)

Audio-wise, the game's pretty richly detailed, and the UI thankfully doesn't have as many stock sounds as the previous game's did. Gunfire and combat overall are pretty punchy. However, I don't know what happened with the game's music, but for whatever reason, has nowhere [i]near[/i] as much impact as Human Revolution's. Like with the new characters mentioned above, the new tracks seem to be... [i]subdued[/i] in the impact they make, like they [i]want[/i] so desperately to hold your attention, but someone or something is holding them back. It's strange, especially considering how effortlessly memorable Human Revolution's soundtrack still is, more than a decade later.

Now for story. This one's tough, since Human Revolution's story was just [i]so good,[/i] and not much was hidden in the game in order to really understand it, save for extra details that go to enhance the characters and world-building even further. In Mankind Divided's case, the main story works well enough to not overstay its welcome or lose the player along the way, but various aspects of it require careful scrutiny, some in-depth investigation in-game, and a decent amount of thought to make it better than just "OK." Where the game truly shines though are its side missions, almost all of which come with fairly interesting storylines and characters. One overarching side mission, however, basically (and frustratingly) goes nowhere, and begs for more details and a satisfying conclusion, especially in a follow-up game. Worse, and insultingly, in said mission's "resolution," the game basically shrugs and tells the player to "figure it out."

Of course, one has to acknowledge the elephant in the room: Mankind Divided was quite painfully [i]obviously[/i] meant to be the middle chapter of an incredible trilogy... that we still have yet to see the finale of. It's also the second of a prequel trilogy to a game that is widely considered to be one of the best ever made. While it does an excellent job of tying into the original game and its predecessor, it still feels... incomplete. While by no means a half-baked rush job, story elements were obviously left out on purpose, likely for a follow-up that may never materialize at this point.

Overall though, despite some glaring problems and issues, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided has aged pretty well. Here's hoping it gets a much-deserved sequel that opens the doors for bigger and better things for the franchise.

I am a huge fan of the original Deus Ex and I really enjoyed Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I was prepared to give this one a lot of slack knowing some of the flaws from other reviews. But the biggest flaw, despite arbitrary microtransactions, questionable optimization, odd blurry faces for certain characters, and a fairly weak story is the fact that the game suffers from awful pacing.

The game starts off promising enough: a huge multilayered deserted building for you to creatively sneak or shoot your way through. The AI, though still a bit on the dumb side, provides a fair challenge and is better at pathing and searching rooms. This means that even though it's the first mission, you can't just jump from cover to cover without having to think critically on how you move past clusters of guards. The sequence finishes with a VERY visually appealing sandstorm, with an unfortunately dumb resolution. Still, it's a great way to start the game and if it featured more of these sequences, I would have considered this game one of my favourites despite the other flaws.

Unfortunately, there are only about 5 areas in the entire game that ever get this complex or interesting. Compared to the original Deus Ex, or even Deus Ex: HR, this is incredibly lacking. After the stellar intro sequence you get introduced to Prague which acts as a sort of 'hub world'. This is where things start to grind to a screeching hault. Despite the beauty of Prague with excellent interior and exterior design, the actual play area is far too cramped and limited. I expected a healthy dose of narrative, but these areas are 90% narrative and 10% exploration and gameplay. You have very little in terms of actual space and freedom, which forces you to complete the game's lacking story instead of going off on your own and discovering interesting tidbits about the world.

The biggest problem with Prague is how it isolates certain key areas. I'm not sure if this was a design or optimization choice but the map makes it seem like Prague is bigger than it actually is. Trully, the area is separated into 2 sections: one ridiculously small and the other considerably larger, with every other destination either being a one-off location or a separate entrance to the larger portion. Each of these areas are separated by a long load time. I could imagine how long it must be for non SSD owners.

Even though the game is at its best when you're sneaking/hacking/exploring, there are some small gripes. For one, the Praxis point system seems half baked. I didn't do every sidequest or find any praxis points in the wild yet I was very close to maxed out near the end of the game. I could only imagine what happened to the poor suckers who actually bought points. Also, I'm not a fan of the new hacking system. Aesthetically it's great and when it works, it works pretty well. However, almost 'requiring' items to be successful with some 4 or 5 rated security terminals seems absurd to me.

But the real sour feeling: Why are unskippable credits still a thing? I get it. Your team worked hard on the game and you're proud of your accomplishment. However, not everyone has 20 minutes of free time to throw away to see names of people they haven't met scroll by slowly. As an insult to injury, they snuck a cutscene in the middle of the credits (which I missed part of because I had no idea) and give you an acheivement for watching the whole thing... I could imagine someone who decided to let the credits run not knowing about the cutscene and completely missing out unless they noticed the acheivement.

Consider this a 'mixed' recommendation. Only get this game on a sale, understand that the game gets better past Prague, and understand that this isn't a 'full experience' and you might find yourself enjoying Mankind Divided. But if you're not a fan of Deus Ex or stealth games, avoid this one completely.

We should clear up the elephant in the room, first. A lot of people will be curious why the game is receiving such high praise from professional reviewers and players yet the same people seem to be upset (with the steam rating currently being "mixed").

1. The publisher shoehorned in a microtransaction system for praxis and credits. The good news is that they did this last minute, so the game is perfectly balanced without the extra resources. I never felt starved for praxis or money, in my playthrough. The bad news is that this probably means the rest of the series will have the same system and might not be so balanced.

This is the primary reason people are saying to wait for the game to become cheaper. I don't know if that will actually do anything but, if the future games are unbalanced, it's easy enough to use something like cheatengine to restore the balance; the game being single player and all.

2. The story is very obviously cut on a cliff hanger to make room for one or more sequels. It's hard to overstate how abrupt the ending is. I felt myself physically lurch forward in my chair, as if my car came to a sudden stop. It's very annoying that they didn't feel like they needed to end gracefully.

However, this shouldn't be a huge detriment to the game. For one, there's plenty of content in the game, as is. I got around 26 hrs of content in one playthrough, doing all of the side-missions. And several of the missions involve branching choices, so there should be some replayability in just seeing new content.

The narrative is also not thin. There are a lot of story threads and tangential characters that fill out the game, despite the main story being cut in half or third for sequels. A number of the side missions should also carry over into the sequel(s) so it's highly-recommended that you do all of them.

---

Those two items aside, the game is a worthy successor to Human Revolution. The gameplay is very similar to the previous game's but with more options and more polish.

One major thing they fixed over the previous game is the main city. Detroit always felt a bit barren. There weren't many NPCs, they didn't really move or interact with each other, and they rarely had anything interesting to say. The levels in this game feel significantly more lived-in and alive. There are still plenty of "dumb" NPCs but at least there are more of them to look like a real population. There are also more NPCs who will be talking about the events in the game or give clues about other characters. In essense, NPCs who feel more like a part of the world.

Aside from the main story, the side missions are very impressive. Many feature unique characters and lengthy missions that can introduce some interesting mechanics. Several also tie into the main story in meaningful ways which makes them seem barely optional. Anyone who just powers through the main story and skips the optional missions is genuinely missing out on a lot of content.

The level design is great. All of the story areas have multiple ways to get in and out. There are also plenty of hidden ways to get to places you might not initially think you can get to, to reward people looking more carefully. Exploring the city is a lot of fun and the game really rewards players who spend the time to look around.

I only really have two complaints about this game (aside from the two in my intro):

1. I wish the designers would have kept the missions more tightly located. The main city is split up into sections that require a lengthy loading screen to move between. Some of the missions have you load in, run around, talk to someone, run back, load, run, talk, run, load, etc. Those missions feel like they spend more time in the loading screen and walking around the city than actually talking or accomplishing some goal. Some of this might be mitigated if you have the game on an SSD but idk.

2. The game seems to punish players more, now, for being a guns-blazing kind of person. I picked up every bit of ammo I ever found for the 10mm, the assault rifle, the battle rifle, and the sniper rifle. I also spent the first 2/3 of the game sneaking everywhere so I barely used any ammo. I finally got bored of that and decided to try to fight out of one of the secured areas with a lot of NPCs. I burned through nearly all of my ammo from the previous 2/3 of the game in just that one fight.

I don't know how it would have been if I had tried to fight through more of the game but it seems like players would quickly be starved for ammo. However, the stealth path leaves a player swimming in ammo, health, and energy resources. So it seems a bit unbalanced; feast or famine, compared to the previous game.

--

Overall, the game is easily worth full price, though I understand people wanting to wait for it to be cheaper. I can't say I recommend getting the season pass, as the "demo" DLC mission wasn't really great. I'll personally be waiting until the DLC gets reviewed to decide if they're worth getting.
